desc:
An array of distinct integers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated: some number of elements was moved from the front to the back (possibly none). So the input looks like [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3] or [1, 2, 3].

An inversion is a pair of indices i < j with nums[i] > nums[j]. Return the number of inversions in nums.

nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]  -> 9   (each of 4,5,6 is above each of 1,2,3)
nums = [1, 2, 3]           -> 0
constraints: All values are distinct and nums is a rotation of an ascending array
hints: A general inversion counter works in O(n log n), but this array has a very special shape. How many sorted runs does it have?
The array is a sorted block of larger values followed by a sorted block of smaller values. Inside each block there are no inversions.

Find the index k where the order breaks (nums[k] < nums[k-1]). Every one of the first k values exceeds every one of the remaining n - k values, so the answer is k * (n - k); if the order never breaks the answer is 0.
editorial: Rotating a sorted array of distinct values yields two ascending blocks: the front block B holds the larger values and the back block A holds the smaller ones. Pairs inside B or inside A are in order. Every pair with one element from B and one from A is inverted, because all of B is larger than all of A.

If the break is at index k (the first index with nums[k] < nums[k-1]), the answer is k * (n - k). With no break the array is already sorted and the answer is 0. One scan, O(n) time and O(1) space; the result is at most n2/4 ≤ 6.25 × 108, which fits in 32 bits.
